literature.headline_zh: 沙粒病毒科本期文献呈现多方向研究进展
literature.lead_zh: 本期沙粒病毒科研究集中呈现以下进展。
key_findings_zh: 该测定证明了对主要谱系细分的检测具有谱系依赖性敏感性,并且在血清和全血样本中保持了敏感性。 [10.1021/acssensors.6c01888]
迄今为止,文献中已记录了 88 例先天性 LCMV 感染病例,全球报告了 5 个供体来源的移植相关集群,涉及 17 名受者。 [PMCID:PMC13809767]
低、季节性的 发病率 以及没有确定的保护生物标志物阻碍了传统的 3 期 疫苗 试验。 [10.1038/s41541-026-01614-6]
因此,Cbl-b 靶向策略有望成为传染病 治疗 的有效辅助手段,特别是与治疗性 疫苗 或其他免疫增强疗法联合使用时。 [10.1007/s00281-026-01097-6]
Travel Med Infect Dis 64:102827 - Palacios GA (2008) 一系列致命的移植相关疾病中的新 沙粒病毒。 [10.1007/978-3-662-72811-6_51]
literature.trend_or_risk_zh: 本期研究方向以入选文献实际覆盖的临床、流行病学、宿主生态、诊断或分子监测主题为准。
literature.lead_en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments.
key_findings_en: The assay demonstrated detection across major lineage subdivisions with lineage-dependent sensitivity and maintained sensitivity in serum and whole blood samples. [10.1021/acssensors.6c01888]

To date, 88 congenital cases of LCMV infection have been documented in the literature, and 5 donor-derived transplant-associated clusters involving 17 recipients have been reported worldwide. [PMCID:PMC13809767]
Low, seasonal incidence, and no identified biomarker of protection hinder traditional Phase 3 vaccine trials. [10.1038/s41541-026-01614-6]

Consequently, Cbl-b-targeting strategies hold promise as potent adjuncts to infectious disease treatments, particularly when combined with therapeutic vaccines or other immune-enhancing therapies. [10.1007/s00281-026-01097-6]

brief_items_zh: 本期沙粒病毒科研究集中呈现以下进展。
该测定证明了对主要谱系细分的检测具有谱系依赖性敏感性,并且在血清和全血样本中保持了敏感性。 [10.1021/acssensors.6c01888]。
迄今为止,文献中已记录了 88 例先天性 LCMV 感染病例,全球报告了 5 个供体来源的移植相关集群,涉及 17 名受者。 [PMCID:PMC13809767]。
低、季节性的 发病率 以及没有确定的保护生物标志物阻碍了传统的 3 期 疫苗 试验。 [10.1038/s41541-026-01614-6]。
因此,Cbl-b 靶向策略有望成为传染病 治疗 的有效辅助手段,特别是与治疗性 疫苗 或其他免疫增强疗法联合使用时。 [10.1007/s00281-026-01097-6]。
brief_items_en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments.
The assay demonstrated detection across major lineage subdivisions with lineage-dependent sensitivity and maintained sensitivity in serum and whole blood samples. [10.1021/acssensors.6c01888].

To date, 88 congenital cases of LCMV infection have been documented in the literature, and 5 donor-derived transplant-associated clusters involving 17 recipients have been reported worldwide. [PMCID:PMC13809767].
Low, seasonal incidence, and no identified biomarker of protection hinder traditional Phase 3 vaccine trials. [10.1038/s41541-026-01614-6].
Consequently, Cbl-b-targeting strategies hold promise as potent adjuncts to infectious disease treatments, particularly when combined with therapeutic vaccines or other immune-enhancing therapies.

literature.en: This reporting window highlights the following research developments. The assay demonstrated detection across major lineage subdivisions with lineage-dependent sensitivity and maintained sensitivity in serum and whole blood samples. [10.1021/acssensors.6c01888]. To date, 88 congenital cases of LCMV infection have been documented in the literature, and 5 donor-derived transplant-associated clusters involving 17 recipients have been reported worldwide. [PMCID:PMC13809767]. Low, seasonal incidence, and no identified biomarker of protection hinder traditional Phase 3 vaccine trials. [10.1038/s41541-026-01614-6]. Consequently, Cbl-b-targeting strategies hold promise as potent adjuncts to infectious disease treatments, particularly when combined with therapeutic vaccines or other immune-enhancing therapies.

papers.title: Diagnostics for Hemorrhagic Fever Viruses: Lassa Fever as an Example.
papers.abstract: Lassa virus (LASV) causes severe hemorrhagic fever across West Africa where the development of rapid, accurate diagnostics remains hindered by the extensive lineage-level genetic diversity and by the limited availability of high-level containment laboratories. We developed a LASV assay using the CRISPR-based Streamlined Highlighting of Infections to Navigate Epidemics (SHINE) platform to enable safe, field-deployable detection. To enable assay development without handling live virus, we established a plasmid-based system that generates LASV RNA controls spanning major viral lineages. Using these surrogate plasmids, we optimized the assay for 32 genetically distinct LASV isolates, demonstrating detection across major lineage subdivisions with lineage-dependent sensitivity. The assay maintained sensitivity in serum and whole blood, and was further evaluated using clinical samples in Nigeria. To reduce subjectivity in strip interpretation, we developed supervised machine-learning models for automated classification of lateral flow results. Together, this integrated diagnostic framework supports field-oriented detection of genetically diverse LASV and provides a broader approach for diagnostic development for high-consequence RNA viruses.

papers.abstract_zh: 拉沙病毒 (LASV) 在整个西非引起严重的出血热,而快速、准确的诊断方法的发展仍然受到广泛的谱系水平遗传多样性和高级遏制实验室的有限可用性的阻碍。我们使用基于 CRISPR 的简化感染突出显示以导航流行病 (SHINE) 平台开发了 LASV 检测,以实现安全、可现场部署的检测。为了在不处理活病毒的情况下进行检测开发,我们建立了一个基于质粒的系统,可以生成跨越主要病毒谱系的 LASV RNA 对照。使用这些替代质粒,我们优化了 32 种遗传上不同的 LASV 分离株的检测方法,证明了跨主要谱系细分的检测具有谱系依赖性灵敏度。该测定保持了血清和全血的灵敏度,并使用尼日利亚的临床样本进行了进一步评估。为了减少条带解释中的主观性,我们开发了监督机器学习模型,用于侧流结果的自动分类。总之,这个集成的诊断框架支持遗传多样性 LASV 的现场定向检测,并为高后果 RNA 病毒的诊断开发提供了更广泛的方法。

papers.title: Late-stage clinical development pathways for Lassa fever vaccines: scientific, operational, and regulatory considerations
papers.abstract: Lassa fever remains a major public health challenge in West Africa, with recurring outbreaks and no licensed vaccine despite a growing pipeline. Low, seasonal incidence, and no identified biomarker of protection hinder traditional Phase 3 vaccine trials. Here, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) explores conventional and alternative clinical and regulatory pathways, with realistic evidence expectations for licensure, to advance Lassa vaccine candidates beyond Phase 2 where Phase 3 efficacy trials may not be feasible.

papers.full_text: AbstractLymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), a rodent-borne mammarenavirus, is endemic worldwide and under-appreciated although it has neurotropism and potential for serious clinical disease. LCMV is commonly carried by the house mouse (Mus musculus), thus being distributed globally in urban and rural areas. Transmission occurs primarily through inhalation of aerosolised excreta from infected rodents or contaminated secretions, with additional routes including solid organ transplantation, rarely, and vertical transmission. In humans, LCMV infection may vary from an inapparent or self-limiting febrile disease to more severe diseases such as aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis especially in immunocompromised patients. Congenital infections have been reported to cause chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications, a variety of neurologic malformations, intellectual disability, neurodevelopmental problems, and death of the foetus. To date, 88 congenital cases of LCMV infection have been documented in the literature, and 5 donor-derived transplant-associated clusters involving 17 recipients have been reported worldwide. The objective of this narrative review is to provide a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of LCMV. Specifically, the review summarizes current knowledge on its virological characteristics, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Particular attention is given to congenital infection, transplant-associated disease, and the evolving epidemiology of LCMV, with emphasis on its public health relevance within a One Health framework. Laboratory approaches and diagnostic challenges are also discussed, including relevant biosafety considerations. Finally, the review highlights persisting knowledge gaps and identifies priority areas for future research, surveillance, and public health action.Keywords: aseptic meningitis, congenital infection, Europe, laboratory diagnosis, LCMV, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, neurotropic zoonosis, organ transplantation 9.DiscussionLCMV is a neglected zoonotic rodent-borne virus distributed around the world that can cause a self-limiting febrile illness, aseptic meningitis or a severe disease after vertical transmission or transmission from a transplant donor (Bonthius, 2024; Gass et al., 2025). It is important to recognize LCMV infection not as rare, but as a relevant neurotropic zoonosis in Europe, albeit underestimated.Epidemiology shows a stable circulation within murine reservoirs, mainly Mus musculus, which is the primary source of human infection (Fornůsková et al., 2021; Mehl et al., 2025; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).Despite substantial progress in the understanding of LCMV biology and disease manifestations, several major knowledge gaps remain. The existing literature is limited by the preponderance of retrospective investigations, outbreak reports, small case series, and case reports and the lack of prospective clinical studies (Fornůsková et al., 2021; Mehl et al., 2025). The true incidence, burden, and geographical distribution of human LCMV infection are still poorly defined, largely because routine surveillance is limited and geographically heterogeneous, and clinical awareness remains suboptimal. These factors may likely lead to an underestimation of the LCMV circulation and are particularly relevant for congenital infection, for which also the full spectrum of long-term outcomes remains incompletely characterized. Additional important knowledge gaps persist regarding human pathogenesis, including the extent to which mechanisms identified in experimental models reflect human infection, particularly in congenital and neurological disease.One of the main challenges in LCMV management is achieving an accurate diagnosis. A single diagnostic test may not provide sufficient sensitivity across all stages of infection, and test performance is strongly influenced by the timing of sample collection. Diagnosis is further complicated by the lack of standardized diagnostic algorithms as well as by the variability in diagnostic methods and case definitions (Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).The fatal LCMV infection in different groups of patients undergoing solid organ transplants from donors who died of apparently non-infectious causes, has further highlighted the pathogenic potential and clinical relevance of this neglected human pathogen. This suggests the need to pay more attention in the transplantation settings (Fischer et al., 2006; MacNeil et al., 2012). Increased awareness of LCMV is warranted among clinicians, as it remains an often-overlooked cause of congenital infection and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. To date, a total of 88 cases of congenital LCMV infection have been reported in the literature, including the two cases recently described in Hungary, underscoring the need for increased awareness of the emerging role of LCMV as a TORCH agent due to its potential impact on maternal, foetal and neonatal health ( (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2011); Ferenc et al., 2022; Koroknai et al., 2024).No specific antiviral treatments or preventive vaccines are available, the general management of LCMV infection is based on the early recognition of the syndrome to be able to modify the intensity of supportive care, treat complications and adjust immunosuppression when necessary (Anesi and Silveira, 2019; Bonthius, 2012; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).The gaps and challenges identified above highlight the need for a broad and multidisciplinary research agenda. Enhanced epidemiological surveillance should be implemented to better define the global distribution and burden of LCMV infection in human and rodent populations. Second, prospective studies are needed to better understand the natural history, clinical spectrum and long-term outcomes of congenital and post-natal infections. Thirdly, there is a need to develop and validate widely accessible and standardized diagnostic tools, in particular for immunocompromised patients and congenital infections. Comparative studies would be particularly helpful to better define the performance of different laboratory methods and specimen types across clinical settings. Further work is also required to elucidate mechanisms of human pathogenesis and to determine the extent to which results obtained in experimental animal models reflect human disease. Finally, the development of antiviral and immunotherapeutic approaches and their clinical evaluation remains an important priority due to the lack of approved therapies for LCMV infection.The main limitation of this review is that it was designed as a narrative rather than a systematic review. In addition, the available literature on LCMV is highly heterogeneous and largely consists of case reports, case series, surveillance studies, and experimental investigations, while prospective clinical studies remain scarce. This heterogeneity limits the comparability of findings across studies and the strength of some conclusions. Nevertheless, this review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis of the evidence currently available on LCMV, integrating recent findings from both human and animal studies, current diagnostic approaches, emerging epidemiological data from different geographical regions, and contemporary considerations regarding biosafety and clinical management. In conclusion, by bringing together virological, clinical, epidemiological, diagnostic, and One Health perspectives, the review provides an integrated framework for understanding the current and evolving public health relevance of LCMV, while highlighting persistent knowledge gaps and key priorities for future research. 1.IntroductionLymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is a worldwide endemic, neglected zoonotic virus transmitted to humans primarily by rodents and can cause a self-limiting febrile illness, aseptic meningitis, or severe disease following organ transplantation or vertical transmission (Bonthius, 2024; Gass et al., 2025).LCMV was isolated in 1933 by Armstrong and Lillie from the cerebrospinal fluid of a patient with meningoencephalitis detected during the St. Louis encephalitis epidemic (St. Louis, Missouri, USA) (Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021b). In 1935, Traub identified the house mouse, Mus musculus, as the natural reservoir host for the virus (Traub, 1935). Key events in the history of LCMV, from its first isolation to the recognition of congenital and transplant-associated disease, are summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Major events of LCMV infection uncovering (created with BioRender).Timeline graphic highlighting key events in LCMV history: first patient identification in Missouri, 1933; mouse as host, 1935; first congenital infection in England, 1955; multiple transplant-related infections in the United States and Australia from 2003 to 2013.Following its discovery, LCMV was recognised as one of the most common causes of aseptic meningitis in humans in the years after. While LCMV is widespread in mice throughout the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe, reports of clinical cases in humans have been relatively rare in recent decades (Flannery et al., 2026). This may be due to non-specific or absent symptoms leading to underdiagnosis and the non-availability of specific diagnostic tests. Thus, the disease has been underestimated, often making it difficult to establish incidence and seroprevalence rates (Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a). House mice are intimately associated with human settlements, but surveillance for LCMV in wild mice in Europe is limited, which calls for an integrated One Health research approach (Mehl et al., 2023; Pankovics et al., 2023). In Europe there is increasing evidence for a more significant widespread ecological and molecular circulation of LCMV than the relatively low number of reported human cases would suggest. This evidence is mainly based on molecular detection and phylogenetic characterization of LCMV in animal reservoirs, particularly wild and pet rodents, which has revealed the presence of multiple viral lineages in different geographical areas, often in the absence of recognised human disease (Charrel et al., 2008; Pankovics et al., 2023; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).The significance of LCMV diagnosis in humans extends beyond sporadic meningitis cases, as several donor-derived infections have been reported in solid organ transplant recipients, presenting with early onset after transplant and rapid progression to multi-organ failure and high mortality (Fischer et al., 2006; MacNeil et al., 2012). Immunosuppression in transplant recipients may mask or delay seroconversion and diagnosis, favoring high viral loads and subsequent systemic rather than neurological complications (Mathur et al., 2017).Another important aspect to consider is the vertical transmission. LCMV infection in pregnancy is associated with severe foetal outcomes including higher morbidity and mortality and is increasingly recognised as a teratogenic human pathogen (Olivieri et al., 2024; Pencole et al., 2022). This narrative review summarizes LCMV biology, epidemiology, and clinical manifestations with a focus on transmission in transplant recipients, risk of congenital infection, and key diagnostic challenges (Olivieri et al., 2024; Pencole et al., 2022). The objective of this narrative review is to provide a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of LCMV. Specifically, the review summarizes current knowledge on its virological characteristics, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Particular attention is given to congenital infection, transplant-associated disease, and the evolving epidemiology of LCMV, with emphasis on its public health relevance within a One Health framework. Laboratory approaches and diagnostic challenges are also discussed, including relevant biosafety considerations. Finally, the review highlights persisting knowledge gaps and identifies priority areas for future research, surveillance, and public health action. 2.Literature search strategy and study selectionA literature search was conducted in the following databases: PubMed, Medline, and Scopus, with no limitations on the year of publication and language. Eligible publications included peer-reviewed original studies, case reports and case series, outbreak and surveillance investigations, clinical studies, relevant animal and in vitro studies, and systematic or narrative reviews. Keywords searched were: lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, epidemiology, seroprevalence, humans, rodents, congenital infection, TORCH, transplant, molecular epidemiology, diagnosis, therapy, immunology, vaccine. Publications were excluded when they were duplicates, lacked sufficient relevant information, or did not contribute to the clinical, epidemiological, diagnostic, therapeutic, biosafety or public health objectives of the review. Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, followed by full-text assessment of key publications. 3.Etiological agentLCMV belongs to the Arenaviridae family, genus Mammarenavirus; it is an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus. The viral particle is round, oval, or pleomorphic, with a diameter of 110–130 nm, and has a typical “sandy” appearance due to the presence of embedded cellular ribosomes. The helical nucleocapsid contains an RNA genome consisting of two ambisense RNA segments (S and L) that encode four viral proteins: the nucleoprotein (NP), the envelope glycoprotein precursor (GPC), which is cleaved into two subunits (GP1 and GP2), the matrix zinc-binding protein (Z), and the L protein as RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). A stable signal peptide (SSP) cleaved during GPC synthesis is also found in the virion spike protein. The organization of the viral particle and its structural proteins is summarized in Figure 2. NP is the main structural protein of arenaviruses, essential for both transcription and replication. Antigens on GP1 are involved in virus neutralization (Pinschewer et al., 2005; Radoshitzky et al., 2023; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a)LCMV uses α-dystroglycan as an important cellular receptor. Receptor-binding affinity and receptor dependence vary substantially among strains and variants. Clone 13, Traub, and WE54 show high-binding affinity to α-dystroglycan, whereas Armstrong, E350, and WE2.2 show substantially lower affinity. In mouse models, high-affinity binding is associated with different tissue tropism, infection of antigen-presenting cells, and viral persistence (Kunz et al., 2001; Smelt et al., 2001). Other LCMV strains can use alternative cell-surface receptors, including heparan sulfate proteoglycans that have been identified as alternative attachment factors for selected low-affinity strains. The observation that there is residual infection in cells lacking both α-dystroglycan and heparan sulfate-related pathways suggests that there might be other entry factors that are not fully characterized (Kunz et al., 2004; Volland et al., 2021). Thus, the high-affinity binding observed in Clone 13 should not be generalized to all LCMV variants or to human clinical isolates.Figure 2Schematic representation of the LCMV viral particle (created with BioRender).Diagram of a spherical virus particle with labeled structural components, including glycoprotein spikes on the envelope, Z matrix protein forming the inner layer, and NP–RNA ribonucleoprotein complexes and L protein polymerases inside the core.During infection, the viral particle binds to the receptors on the cell surface and is internalized by endocytosis. Transcription and replication are confined to the cytoplasm of infected cells. The S RNA encodes an NP in the negative sense and a GPC in the positive sense, which is post-translationally cleaved into GP1 and GP2. The RNA encodes an RdRp in the negative sense and a Z protein in the positive sense, which binds to the RNP complex. The viruses subsequently bud from the plasma membrane, incorporating host lipids into the viral membrane (Rollin et al., 2015). 4.EpidemiologyHuman infection with LCMV is mainly acquired by zoonotic transmission from rodents. The global distribution of LCMV is associated with the distribution of the primary reservoir, the house mouse, Mus musculus (including subspecies). Although LCMV has been detected in multiple regions worldwide, localized clustering of infected rodent populations has been reported and may reflect host ecology and persistent infection within rodent populations (Jezkova et al., 2026). Mice infected in the prenatal period are unable to develop an immune response, develop a chronic asymptomatic infection and shed large quantities of the virus in nasal secretions, saliva, milk, semen, urine and feces (Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).Other rodents, including rats, hamsters and guinea pigs, may also become infected; however, their role as maintenance hosts and the duration of viral shedding are less well established than for Mus musculus. Prolonged shedding may increase opportunities for contamination and exposure, but does not by itself demonstrate prolonged environmental persistence or a substantial burden of human clinical disease (Fornůsková et al., 2021; Mehl et al., 2025). Zoonotic transmission to humans is through inhalation of contaminated aerosols/dust, direct contact with excreta or contamination of food/surfaces or bites. There have been reports of human-to-human transmission in the context of organ transplantation or mother-to-foetus transmission (Amman et al., 2007; Centers for Disease Control (CDC), 1984).There are five phylogenetic lineages of LCMV, numbered from I to V, with lineages I and II being the most commonly detected worldwide (Albariño et al., 2010; Fornůsková et al., 2021). full_text_sections.discussion: 9.DiscussionLCMV is a neglected zoonotic rodent-borne virus distributed around the world that can cause a self-limiting febrile illness, aseptic meningitis or a severe disease after vertical transmission or transmission from a transplant donor (Bonthius, 2024; Gass et al., 2025). It is important to recognize LCMV infection not as rare, but as a relevant neurotropic zoonosis in Europe, albeit underestimated.Epidemiology shows a stable circulation within murine reservoirs, mainly Mus musculus, which is the primary source of human infection (Fornůsková et al., 2021; Mehl et al., 2025; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).Despite substantial progress in the understanding of LCMV biology and disease manifestations, several major knowledge gaps remain. The existing literature is limited by the preponderance of retrospective investigations, outbreak reports, small case series, and case reports and the lack of prospective clinical studies (Fornůsková et al., 2021; Mehl et al., 2025). The true incidence, burden, and geographical distribution of human LCMV infection are still poorly defined, largely because routine surveillance is limited and geographically heterogeneous, and clinical awareness remains suboptimal. These factors may likely lead to an underestimation of the LCMV circulation and are particularly relevant for congenital infection, for which also the full spectrum of long-term outcomes remains incompletely characterized. Additional important knowledge gaps persist regarding human pathogenesis, including the extent to which mechanisms identified in experimental models reflect human infection, particularly in congenital and neurological disease.One of the main challenges in LCMV management is achieving an accurate diagnosis. A single diagnostic test may not provide sufficient sensitivity across all stages of infection, and test performance is strongly influenced by the timing of sample collection. Diagnosis is further complicated by the lack of standardized diagnostic algorithms as well as by the variability in diagnostic methods and case definitions (Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).The fatal LCMV infection in different groups of patients undergoing solid organ transplants from donors who died of apparently non-infectious causes, has further highlighted the pathogenic potential and clinical relevance of this neglected human pathogen. This suggests the need to pay more attention in the transplantation settings (Fischer et al., 2006; MacNeil et al., 2012). Increased awareness of LCMV is warranted among clinicians, as it remains an often-overlooked cause of congenital infection and neurodevelopmental abnormalities. To date, a total of 88 cases of congenital LCMV infection have been reported in the literature, including the two cases recently described in Hungary, underscoring the need for increased awareness of the emerging role of LCMV as a TORCH agent due to its potential impact on maternal, foetal and neonatal health ( (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2011); Ferenc et al., 2022; Koroknai et al., 2024).No specific antiviral treatments or preventive vaccines are available, the general management of LCMV infection is based on the early recognition of the syndrome to be able to modify the intensity of supportive care, treat complications and adjust immunosuppression when necessary (Anesi and Silveira, 2019; Bonthius, 2012; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).The gaps and challenges identified above highlight the need for a broad and multidisciplinary research agenda. Enhanced epidemiological surveillance should be implemented to better define the global distribution and burden of LCMV infection in human and rodent populations. Second, prospective studies are needed to better understand the natural history, clinical spectrum and long-term outcomes of congenital and post-natal infections. Thirdly, there is a need to develop and validate widely accessible and standardized diagnostic tools, in particular for immunocompromised patients and congenital infections. Comparative studies would be particularly helpful to better define the performance of different laboratory methods and specimen types across clinical settings. Further work is also required to elucidate mechanisms of human pathogenesis and to determine the extent to which results obtained in experimental animal models reflect human disease. Finally, the development of antiviral and immunotherapeutic approaches and their clinical evaluation remains an important priority due to the lack of approved therapies for LCMV infection.The main limitation of this review is that it was designed as a narrative rather than a systematic review. In addition, the available literature on LCMV is highly heterogeneous and largely consists of case reports, case series, surveillance studies, and experimental investigations, while prospective clinical studies remain scarce. This heterogeneity limits the comparability of findings across studies and the strength of some conclusions. Nevertheless, this review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date synthesis of the evidence currently available on LCMV, integrating recent findings from both human and animal studies, current diagnostic approaches, emerging epidemiological data from different geographical regions, and contemporary considerations regarding biosafety and clinical management. In conclusion, by bringing together virological, clinical, epidemiological, diagnostic, and One Health perspectives, the review provides an integrated framework for understanding the current and evolving public health relevance of LCMV, while highlighting persistent knowledge gaps and key priorities for future research.
full_text_sections.other: 1.IntroductionLymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is a worldwide endemic, neglected zoonotic virus transmitted to humans primarily by rodents and can cause a self-limiting febrile illness, aseptic meningitis, or severe disease following organ transplantation or vertical transmission (Bonthius, 2024; Gass et al., 2025).LCMV was isolated in 1933 by Armstrong and Lillie from the cerebrospinal fluid of a patient with meningoencephalitis detected during the St. Louis encephalitis epidemic (St. Louis, Missouri, USA) (Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021b). In 1935, Traub identified the house mouse, Mus musculus, as the natural reservoir host for the virus (Traub, 1935). Key events in the history of LCMV, from its first isolation to the recognition of congenital and transplant-associated disease, are summarized in Figure 1.Figure 1Major events of LCMV infection uncovering (created with BioRender).Timeline graphic highlighting key events in LCMV history: first patient identification in Missouri, 1933; mouse as host, 1935; first congenital infection in England, 1955; multiple transplant-related infections in the United States and Australia from 2003 to 2013.Following its discovery, LCMV was recognised as one of the most common causes of aseptic meningitis in humans in the years after. While LCMV is widespread in mice throughout the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Europe, reports of clinical cases in humans have been relatively rare in recent decades (Flannery et al., 2026). This may be due to non-specific or absent symptoms leading to underdiagnosis and the non-availability of specific diagnostic tests. Thus, the disease has been underestimated, often making it difficult to establish incidence and seroprevalence rates (Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a). House mice are intimately associated with human settlements, but surveillance for LCMV in wild mice in Europe is limited, which calls for an integrated One Health research approach (Mehl et al., 2023; Pankovics et al., 2023). In Europe there is increasing evidence for a more significant widespread ecological and molecular circulation of LCMV than the relatively low number of reported human cases would suggest. This evidence is mainly based on molecular detection and phylogenetic characterization of LCMV in animal reservoirs, particularly wild and pet rodents, which has revealed the presence of multiple viral lineages in different geographical areas, often in the absence of recognised human disease (Charrel et al., 2008; Pankovics et al., 2023; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a).The significance of LCMV diagnosis in humans extends beyond sporadic meningitis cases, as several donor-derived infections have been reported in solid organ transplant recipients, presenting with early onset after transplant and rapid progression to multi-organ failure and high mortality (Fischer et al., 2006; MacNeil et al., 2012). Immunosuppression in transplant recipients may mask or delay seroconversion and diagnosis, favoring high viral loads and subsequent systemic rather than neurological complications (Mathur et al., 2017).Another important aspect to consider is the vertical transmission. LCMV infection in pregnancy is associated with severe foetal outcomes including higher morbidity and mortality and is increasingly recognised as a teratogenic human pathogen (Olivieri et al., 2024; Pencole et al., 2022). This narrative review summarizes LCMV biology, epidemiology, and clinical manifestations with a focus on transmission in transplant recipients, risk of congenital infection, and key diagnostic challenges (Olivieri et al., 2024; Pencole et al., 2022). The objective of this narrative review is to provide a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of LCMV. Specifically, the review summarizes current knowledge on its virological characteristics, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Particular attention is given to congenital infection, transplant-associated disease, and the evolving epidemiology of LCMV, with emphasis on its public health relevance within a One Health framework. Laboratory approaches and diagnostic challenges are also discussed, including relevant biosafety considerations. Finally, the review highlights persisting knowledge gaps and identifies priority areas for future research, surveillance, and public health action. 2.Literature search strategy and study selectionA literature search was conducted in the following databases: PubMed, Medline, and Scopus, with no limitations on the year of publication and language. Eligible publications included peer-reviewed original studies, case reports and case series, outbreak and surveillance investigations, clinical studies, relevant animal and in vitro studies, and systematic or narrative reviews. Keywords searched were: lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, epidemiology, seroprevalence, humans, rodents, congenital infection, TORCH, transplant, molecular epidemiology, diagnosis, therapy, immunology, vaccine. Publications were excluded when they were duplicates, lacked sufficient relevant information, or did not contribute to the clinical, epidemiological, diagnostic, therapeutic, biosafety or public health objectives of the review. Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance, followed by full-text assessment of key publications. 3.Etiological agentLCMV belongs to the Arenaviridae family, genus Mammarenavirus; it is an enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA virus. The viral particle is round, oval, or pleomorphic, with a diameter of 110–130 nm, and has a typical “sandy” appearance due to the presence of embedded cellular ribosomes. The helical nucleocapsid contains an RNA genome consisting of two ambisense RNA segments (S and L) that encode four viral proteins: the nucleoprotein (NP), the envelope glycoprotein precursor (GPC), which is cleaved into two subunits (GP1 and GP2), the matrix zinc-binding protein (Z), and the L protein as RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp). A stable signal peptide (SSP) cleaved during GPC synthesis is also found in the virion spike protein. The organization of the viral particle and its structural proteins is summarized in Figure 2. NP is the main structural protein of arenaviruses, essential for both transcription and replication. Antigens on GP1 are involved in virus neutralization (Pinschewer et al., 2005; Radoshitzky et al., 2023; Vilibić-Čavlek et al., 2021a)LCMV uses α-dystroglycan as an important cellular receptor. Receptor-binding affinity and receptor dependence vary substantially among strains and variants. Clone 13, Traub, and WE54 show high-binding affinity to α-dystroglycan, whereas Armstrong, E350, and WE2.2 show substantially lower affinity. In mouse models, high-affinity binding is associated with different tissue tropism, infection of antigen-presenting cells, and viral persistence (Kunz et al., 2001; Smelt et al., 2001). Other LCMV strains can use alternative cell-surface receptors, including heparan sulfate proteoglycans that have been identified as alternative attachment factors for selected low-affinity strains. The observation that there is residual infection in cells lacking both α-dystroglycan and heparan sulfate-related pathways suggests that there might be other entry factors that are not fully characterized (Kunz et al., 2004; Volland et al., 2021). Thus, the high-affinity binding observed in Clone 13 should not be generalized to all LCMV variants or to human clinical isolates.Figure 2Schematic representation of the LCMV viral particle (created with BioRender).Diagram of a spherical virus particle with labeled structural components, including glycoprotein spikes on the envelope, Z matrix protein forming the inner layer, and NP–RNA ribonucleoprotein complexes and L protein polymerases inside the core.During infection, the viral particle binds to the receptors on the cell surface and is internalized by endocytosis. papers.title: The role of Cbl-b: relationship between cancer and infectious disease
papers.abstract: Casitas B-cell lymphoma-b protein (Cbl-b) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that negatively regulates signaling pathways. Although it is involved in the maintenance of immune homeostasis, Cbl-b may also be exploited by tumors or pathogens, leading to immune evasion and persistent infection. In recent years, the role of Cbl-b in tumor immunotherapy has been progressively elucidated, with related Cbl-b inhibitors (such as NX-1607) advancing into clinical trials. It has also been found that Cbl-b inhibition or knockout enhances host immune responses in infection models, such as lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) and Candida albicans infection models. Consequently, Cbl-b-targeting strategies hold promise as potent adjuncts to infectious disease treatments, particularly when combined with therapeutic vaccines or other immune-enhancing therapies. Given the immunological parallels between infection and tumorigenesis, this review examines the immunoregulatory role of Cbl-b in both contexts and compares their similarities and differences. Additionally, this review summarizes currently available mainstream Cbl-b-targeting strategies to provide new insights for the application of Cbl-b in immunotherapy for infectious diseases.

papers.abstract_zh: Casitas B 细胞淋巴瘤-b 蛋白 (Cbl-b) 是一种 E3 泛素连接酶,可负向调节信号通路。尽管 Cbl-b 参与维持免疫稳态,但它也可能被肿瘤或病原体利用,导致免疫逃避和持续感染。近年来,Cbl-b在肿瘤免疫治疗中的作用逐渐被阐明,相关Cbl-b抑制剂(如NX-1607)也进入临床试验。还发现Cbl-b抑制或敲除可增强感染模型中的宿主 免疫应答,例如淋巴细胞脉络丛脑膜炎病毒 (LCMV)和白色念珠菌感染模型。因此,Cbl-b 靶向策略有望成为传染病 治疗 的有效辅助手段,特别是与治疗性 疫苗 或其他免疫增强疗法联合使用时。鉴于感染和肿瘤发生之间的免疫学相似性,本综述检查了 Cbl-b 在这两种情况下的免疫调节作用,并比较了它们的异同。此外,本文还总结了目前主流的Cbl-b靶向策略,为Cbl-b在传染病免疫治疗中的应用提供新的见解。

papers.title: Progressive SLAMF7 downregulation is associated with terminal CD8 T-cell exhaustion and aggressive disease in renal cell carcinoma
papers.abstract: T-cell exhaustion is a dysfunctional state under persistent antigenic stimulation in chronic viral infections and tumors. Although immune checkpoint blockade can reinvigorate exhausted T cells, responses remain limited, emphasizing the need to better understand exhaustion. SLAMF7 is an immune-regulatory receptor, but its regulatory and functional role during CD8 + T-cell exhaustion remains unclear. Here, we reported that SLAMF7 was absent in naïve mouse and human CD8 T cells but was induced upon in vitro activation. Following acute lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection, all effector and memory subsets expressed SLAMF7, with higher levels in more differentiated cytolytic populations. Under persistent antigenic stimulation, including chronic LCMV infection, murine tumor models, human renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and non-small cell lung cancer, SLAMF7 was highly expressed in progenitor and transitory exhausted subsets but downregulated in PD-1 hi terminally exhausted cells. This downregulation coincided with increased inhibitory receptor and TOX expression, attenuated cytotoxic and polyfunctional responses, and progressive epigenetic remodeling toward terminal exhaustion-associated chromatin programs. Furthermore, SLAMF7 deficiency impaired CD8 + T-cell expansion and antitumor activity. Across models, SLAMF7 downregulation was more closely associated with prolonged antigen exposure than with antigen burden. In RCC patients, SLAMF7-based stratification revealed distinct immunological states: SLAMF7-HI tumors retained progenitor-like CD8 T cells with preserved effector function, whereas SLAMF7-DN tumors were enriched for terminally exhausted cells and associated with high nuclear grade. Collectively, these findings identify SLAMF7 downregulation as a marker of terminal CD8 T-cell exhaustion and suggest its potential as a biomarker of immune competence and disease severity.

elements_en.research_question_and_background: T-cell exhaustion is a dysfunctional state under persistent antigenic stimulation in chronic viral infections and tumors. Although immune checkpoint blockade can reinvigorate exhausted T cells, responses remain limited, emphasizing the need to better understand exhaustion.
elements_en.study_design_and_population: The study involved the examination of SLAMF7 expression in CD8 T cells from naïve and activated mouse and human cells, as well as in various models of persistent antigenic stimulation, including chronic LCMV infection, murine tumor models, human renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and non-small cell lung cancer.
elements_en.methods: SLAMF7 expression was assessed in naïve and activated mouse and human CD8 T cells, as well as in various models of persistent antigenic stimulation. The study utilized in vitro activation, chronic LCMV infection, and tumor models to investigate SLAMF7 expression and its association with T-cell exhaustion and disease progression.
elements_en.main_results: SLAMF7 was absent in naïve mouse and human CD8 T cells but was induced upon in vitro activation. Following acute LCMV infection, all effector and memory subsets expressed SLAMF7, with higher levels in more differentiated cytolytic populations. In persistent antigenic stimulation, SLAMF7 was highly expressed in progenitor and transitory exhausted subsets but downregulated in PD-1 hi terminally exhausted cells. This downregulation coincided with increased inhibitory receptor and TOX expression, attenuated cytotoxic and polyfunctional responses, and progressive epigenetic remodeling toward terminal exhaustion-associated chromatin programs.
elements_en.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings identify SLAMF7 downregulation as a marker of terminal CD8 T-cell exhaustion and suggest its potential as a biomarker of immune competence and disease severity.
elements_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: SLAMF7 downregulation is associated with terminal CD8 T-cell exhaustion and aggressive disease in renal cell carcinoma, which can inform surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment strategies for cancer patients.
elements_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of non-randomized models and the need for further validation in larger clinical cohorts. The evidence strength is moderate due to the use of multiple models and patient samples, but the findings are cautiously informative for future research and clinical applications.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: T 细胞耗竭是慢性病毒感染和肿瘤中持续抗原刺激下的一种功能障碍状态。尽管免疫检查点阻断可以使疲惫的 T 细胞重新焕发活力,但反应仍然有限,这强调需要更好地了解疲惫状态。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究涉及检查来自幼稚和激活的小鼠和人类细胞的 CD8 T 细胞以及各种持续抗原刺激模型(包括慢性 LCMV 感染、小鼠肿瘤模型、人肾细胞癌 (RCC) 和非小细胞肺癌)中 SLAMF7 的表达。
elements_zh.methods: 在初始和激活的小鼠和人类 CD8 T 细胞以及各种持续抗原刺激模型中评估了 SLAMF7 的表达。该研究利用体外激活、慢性 LCMV 感染和肿瘤模型来研究 SLAMF7 表达及其与 T 细胞耗竭和疾病进展的关系。
elements_zh.main_results: SLAMF7 在初始小鼠和人类 CD8 T 细胞中不存在,但在体外激活后被诱导。急性 LCMV 感染后,所有效应子和记忆亚群均表达 SLAMF7,在分化程度更高的溶细胞群体中表达水平更高。在持续抗原刺激中,SLAMF7 在祖细胞和暂时衰竭细胞亚群中高表达,但在 PD-1 hi 终末衰竭细胞中下调。这种下调与抑制性受体和 TOX 表达的增加、细胞毒性和多功能反应的减弱以及最终耗竭相关染色质程序的渐进表观遗传重塑相一致。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现将 SLAMF7 下调确定为终末 CD8 T 细胞耗竭的标志,并表明其作为免疫能力和疾病严重程度的生物标志物的潜力。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: SLAMF7 下调与肾细胞癌中终末 CD8 T 细胞耗竭和侵袭性疾病相关,这可以为癌症患者的 监测、诊断 和 治疗 策略提供参考。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的局限性包括使用非随机模型以及需要在更大的临床 队列研究 中进一步验证。由于使用了多个模型和患者样本,证据强度中等,但研究结果为未来的研究和临床应用提供了谨慎的信息。

papers.title_zh: 进行性 SLAMF7 下调与肾细胞癌终末 CD8 T 细胞耗竭和侵袭性疾病相关
papers.source_body_en: T-cell exhaustion is a dysfunctional state under persistent antigenic stimulation in chronic viral infections and tumors. Although immune checkpoint blockade can reinvigorate exhausted T cells, responses remain limited, emphasizing the need to better understand exhaustion. SLAMF7 is an immune-regulatory receptor, but its regulatory and functional role during CD8 + T-cell exhaustion remains unclear. Here, we reported that SLAMF7 was absent in naïve mouse and human CD8 T cells but was induced upon in vitro activation. Following acute lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection, all effector and memory subsets expressed SLAMF7, with higher levels in more differentiated cytolytic populations. Under persistent antigenic stimulation, including chronic LCMV infection, murine tumor models, human renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and non-small cell lung cancer, SLAMF7 was highly expressed in progenitor and transitory exhausted subsets but downregulated in PD-1 hi terminally exhausted cells. This downregulation coincided with increased inhibitory receptor and TOX expression, attenuated cytotoxic and polyfunctional responses, and progressive epigenetic remodeling toward terminal exhaustion-associated chromatin programs. Furthermore, SLAMF7 deficiency impaired CD8 + T-cell expansion and antitumor activity. Across models, SLAMF7 downregulation was more closely associated with prolonged antigen exposure than with antigen burden. In RCC patients, SLAMF7-based stratification revealed distinct immunological states: SLAMF7-HI tumors retained progenitor-like CD8 T cells with preserved effector function, whereas SLAMF7-DN tumors were enriched for terminally exhausted cells and associated with high nuclear grade. Collectively, these findings identify SLAMF7 downregulation as a marker of terminal CD8 T-cell exhaustion and suggest its potential as a biomarker of immune competence and disease severity.
papers.abstract_zh: T 细胞耗竭是慢性病毒感染和肿瘤中持续抗原刺激下的一种功能障碍状态。尽管免疫检查点阻断可以使疲惫的 T 细胞重新焕发活力,但反应仍然有限,这强调需要更好地了解疲惫状态。SLAMF7 是一种免疫调节受体,但其在 CD8 + T 细胞耗竭过程中的调节和功能作用仍不清楚。在这里,我们报道了 SLAMF7 在幼稚小鼠和人类 CD8 T 细胞中不存在,但在体外激活时被诱导。急性 淋巴细胞脉络丛脑膜炎病毒 (LCMV) 感染后,所有效应子和记忆亚群均表达 SLAMF7,且在分化程度较高的溶细胞群体中表达水平较高。在持续的抗原刺激下,包括慢性 LCMV 感染、小鼠肿瘤模型、人肾细胞癌 (RCC) 和非小细胞肺癌,SLAMF7 在祖细胞和暂时衰竭细胞亚群中高表达,但在 PD-1 hi 终末衰竭细胞中下调。这种下调与抑制性受体和 TOX 表达的增加、细胞毒性和多功能反应的减弱以及最终耗竭相关染色质程序的渐进表观遗传重塑相一致。此外,SLAMF7 缺陷会损害 CD8 + T 细胞的扩增和抗肿瘤活性。在各个模型中,SLAMF7 下调与抗原暴露时间延长的关系比与抗原负荷的关系更密切。在 RCC 患者中,基于 SLAMF7 的分层揭示了不同的免疫状态:SLAMF7-HI 肿瘤保留了祖细胞样 CD8 T 细胞,且保留了效应器功能,而 SLAMF7-DN 肿瘤富含最终耗尽的细胞,并与高核级别相关。总的来说,这些发现将 SLAMF7 下调确定为终末 CD8 T 细胞耗竭的标志物,并表明其作为免疫能力和疾病严重程度的生物标志物的潜力。

papers.full_text: Zusammenfassung Arenaviren tragen ein segmentiertes RNA-Genom, das Leserahmen mit beiden Polaritäten enthält (Ambisense- Kodierungsstrategie). Die Viren werden von Nagetieren auf den Menschen übertragen und können schwere Erkrankungen auslösen. Das Lassa-Virus und weitere afrikanische und südamerikanische Arenaviren verursachen hämorrhagische Fieber mit zum Teil tödlichem Verlauf. Das Lymphozytäre Choriomeningitis-Virus (LCMV) kommt weltweit vor und kann bei immunkompetenten Personen eine aseptische Meningitis auslösen. Nach LCMV-Übertragung auf immunsupprimierte Patienten kommt es zu tödlichen Verläufen, die kongenitale Infektion kann zu Fehlbildungen des fetalen Gehirns führen. LCMV ist außerdem ein wichtiges Modellpathogen für immunologische Studien. Zusammenfassung Arenaviren tragen ein segmentiertes RNA-Genom, das Leserahmen mit beiden Polaritäten enthält (Ambisense- Kodierungsstrategie). Die Viren werden von Nagetieren auf den Menschen übertragen und können schwere Erkrankungen auslösen. Das Lassa-Virus und weitere afrikanische und südamerikanische Arenaviren verursachen hämorrhagische Fieber mit zum Teil tödlichem Verlauf. Das Lymphozytäre Choriomeningitis-Virus (LCMV) kommt weltweit vor und kann bei immunkompetenten Personen eine aseptische Meningitis auslösen. Nach LCMV-Übertragung auf immunsupprimierte Patienten kommt es zu tödlichen Verläufen, die kongenitale Infektion kann zu Fehlbildungen des fetalen Gehirns führen. LCMV ist außerdem ein wichtiges Modellpathogen für immunologische Studien. View UK invests £33.2m in vaccines to tackle future epidemic threats Share this page The funding will support eight projects targeting diseases including Ebola, Marburg, Lassa fever, plague, Nipah virus, chikungunya and Mayaro. The projects will focus on developing promising vaccines, advancing clinical trials and creating technologies that could make vaccine design and manufacture faster and more effective. Delivered through Innovate UK and supported by the UK Vaccine Network, the programme is designed to strengthen the UK’s ability to develop, test and deploy vaccines rapidly when new outbreaks emerge. It will also support vaccine development and access in low- and middle-income countries, where infectious disease outbreaks can have a particularly severe impact. The government said investing before an outbreak occurs could reduce response times and strengthen resilience against future health emergencies. The programme has previously supported the development of the Oxford/AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine, demonstrating the potential value of preparing vaccine technologies before a pandemic takes hold. Health Minister for Science, Innovation and Investment Chris McDonald said: ‘The world remains at risk from new and re-emerging infectious diseases, and outbreaks overseas can quickly become threats to people here at home. ‘This £33.2 million investment will back leading scientists to develop and deploy vaccines faster and strengthen our pandemic preparedness while supporting our world-leading life sciences sector. ‘By investing before a crisis hits, we can better protect the public, save lives and ensure the UK is ready to respond to future threats.’ The need for continued research has been highlighted by recent outbreaks of serious infectious diseases. Ebola has an average case-fatality rate of around 50%, while Marburg outbreaks were reported in Rwanda in 2024 and Tanzania in 2025. There is currently no approved Marburg vaccine or antiviral treatment. The government also pointed to recent reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case linked to a laboratory worker’s death in Russia’s Irkutsk region, where almost 200 contacts were reportedly placed under precautionary medical observation. The eight new projects will build research, clinical trial and technical capacity so vaccines can be developed and manufactured at speed when new threats emerge. Ministers said the investment would help ensure vaccines are affordable and accessible in countries most at risk, while reducing the potential for overseas outbreaks to develop into wider international threats. The funding reflects a shift towards preparing for future pandemics before they occur, rather than relying solely on emergency responses once an outbreak is already under way. Chief Medical Officer for England Professor Sir Chris Whitty said: ‘These projects aim to prevent some of the most dangerous infectious diseases in the world today. ‘The development of safe and effective vaccines for these diseases will strengthen our ability to protect people around the world.’ Get the latest from our social media Your subscription could not be saved. news.content_title: Lagos unveils digital Bioshield to tackle emerging disease threats
news.content: Saturday, November 28, 2026 Follow Us on Google Search Home National Columns Business China News Politics & Power Opinion Entertainment The Sun TV Sporting Sun The Sun Foundation Lagos unveils digital Bioshield to tackle emerging disease threats 26 November 2026 12:46 am WAT By Doris Obinna Follow Us on Google ...Seeks Africa-wide alliance to strengthen health security Lagos State Government has unveiled a digital biosecurity system powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and telemedicine to detect and contain emerging disease threats while keeping businesses and economic activities running during public health emergen cies. The initiative, known as Lagos State Bioshield, is designed to strengthen disease surveillance, identify potential infections early and prevent outbreaks from disrupting livelihoods in Nigeria’s commercial hub. Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, unveiled the framework at the 11th African Conference on One Health and Biosecurity, organised by the state government in partnership with the Global Emerging Pathogens Treatment Consortium (GET Consortium) at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. Speaking at the conference themed, “Bio-Shielding Africa’s Megacities Against Emerging Threats: The Lagos State Story,” Abayomi said the initiative was developed from lessons learnt during the Ebola outbreak and COVID-19 pandemic, particularly the need to protect public health without shutting down economic activities. He said closing Lagos during an epidemic could have devastating consequences, considering that about 70 per cent of residents depend on daily earnings for survival. According to him, the Bioshield would enable businesses, tourism, social activities and other economic engagements to continue while the government monitors and responds to biological threats. He identified Lassa fever, dengue, yellow fever, Marburg virus disease and Ebola, as well as emerging and unknown pathogens, as threats requiring stronger preparedness. Abayomi said Lagos’ estimated 30.1 million population, high population density, rapid urbanisation, migration and international travel exposed the state to heightened outbreak risks. He disclosed that Lagos receives about 70 per cent of Nigeria’s international air traffic and approximately 1.8 million cattle annually, stressing the need for an integrated approach covering human, animal and environmental health. Explaining how the system works, the commissioner said its two-layer structure monitors potential biological threats at entry points and tracks individuals who develop symptoms after arriving in the state. Its Health Radar platform uses WhatsApp, SMS and email to register and monitor travellers and participants at major events, conducting daily health checks for up to 21 days. Individuals reporting symptoms are connected to telemedicine services for initial assessment, with laboratory investigations, referrals and other interventions activated where necessary. Abayomi disclosed that the technology was successfully deployed during the recently concluded CANEX WKND, monitoring about 19,000 registered delegates, including 2,298 international visitors, amid concerns over Ebola outbreaks in Central Africa. The exercise recorded 2,454 telemedicine consultations, 241 clinical referrals and 219 individuals flagged for further attention. He said all identified cases were followed up and closed out, with no severe outcome linked to the suspected high-consequence infections reported. He said the state was developing Bioshield 3.0 to improve artificial intelligence and telemedicine capabilities, strengthen integration with airports and event centres and establish sustainable financing and legal frameworks. Special Adviser to the Governor on Health, Dr. Kemi Ogunyemi, described Lagos as a critical gateway for biological threats entering Africa, given its population, seaports, international airport and commercial activities. She called for an Africa-wide BioShield Alliance involving megacities such as Lagos, Cairo, Kinshasa, Johannesburg and Nairobi to promote data sharing, joint training and common preparedness standards. Earlier, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Health, Dr. Dayo Lajide, said lessons from the 2014 Ebola outbreak and COVID-19 had strengthened the state’s commitment to preparedness. She cited investments in a Biosafety Level 3 laboratory and biobank at the Infectious Disease Hospital, Yaba, alongside intensified surveillance and healthcare workers’ training. In his keynote address, Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic), Lagos State University of Science and Technology, Prof. Abiodun Denloye, identified poor sanitation, unsafe water, inadequate housing and environmental degradation as factors worsening disease vulnerability in African cities. He advocated stronger environmental protection, disease surveillance, resilient urban planning, community protection and One Health governance. Also, GET Consortium’s Chief Operating Officer, Dr. Ayodotun Bobadoye, called for sustained investment in laboratory infrastructure, border monitoring, workforce development and community engagement. Director General, Nigerian Institute of Medical Research (NIMR), Prof. John Obafunwa, urged increased local investment in medical research, genomic sequencing, vaccine development and domestic production of essential medical supplies to reduce Africa’s dependence on imports. The conference brought together policymakers, researchers and health professionals to strengthen Africa’s preparedness against emerging biological threats. The initiative, known as Lagos State Bioshield, is designed to strengthen disease surveillance, identify potential infections early and prevent outbreaks from disrupting livelihoods in Nigeria’s commercial hub. Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, unveiled the framework at the 11th African Conference on One Health and Biosecurity, organised by the state government in partnership with the Global Emerging Pathogens Treatment Consortium (GET Consortium) at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. Speaking at the conference themed, “Bio-Shielding Africa’s Megacities Against Emerging Threats: The Lagos State Story,” Abayomi said the initiative was developed from lessons learnt during the Ebola outbreak and COVID-19 pandemic, particularly the need to protect public health without shutting down economic activities. He said closing Lagos during an epidemic could have devastating consequences, considering that about 70 per cent of residents depend on daily earnings for survival. According to him, the Bioshield would enable businesses, tourism, social activities and other economic engagements to continue while the government monitors and responds to biological threats. He identified Lassa fever, dengue, yellow fever, Marburg virus disease and Ebola, as well as emerging and unknown pathogens, as threats requiring stronger preparedness. Abayomi said Lagos’ estimated 30.1 million population, high population density, rapid urbanisation, migration and international travel exposed the state to heightened outbreak risks. He disclosed that Lagos receives about 70 per cent of Nigeria’s international air traffic and approximately 1.8 million cattle annually, stressing the need for an integrated approach covering human, animal and environmental health. Explaining how the system works, the commissioner said its two-layer structure monitors potential biological threats at entry points and tracks individuals who develop symptoms after arriving in the state. Its Health Radar platform uses WhatsApp, SMS and email to register and monitor travellers and participants at major events, conducting daily health checks for up to 21 days. Individuals reporting symptoms are connected to telemedicine services for initial assessment, with laboratory investigations, referrals and other interventions activated where necessary. Abayomi disclosed that the technology was successfully deployed during the recently concluded CANEX WKND, monitoring about 19,000 registered delegates, including 2,298 international visitors, amid concerns over Ebola outbreaks in Central Africa. The exercise recorded 2,454 telemedicine consultations, 241 clinical referrals and 219 individuals flagged for further attention. He said all identified cases were followed up and closed out, with no severe outcome linked to the suspected high-consequence infections reported. He said the state was developing Bioshield 3.0 to improve artificial intelligence and telemedicine capabilities, strengthen integration with airports and event centres and establish sustainable financing and legal frameworks. Special Adviser to the Governor on Health, Dr. Kemi Ogunyemi, described Lagos as a critical gateway for biological threats entering Africa, given its population, seaports, international airport and commercial activities. She called for an Africa-wide BioShield Alliance involving megacities such as Lagos, Cairo, Kinshasa, Johannesburg and Nairobi to promote data sharing, joint training and common preparedness standards. Earlier, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Health, Dr. Dayo Lajide, said lessons from the 2014 Ebola outbreak and COVID-19 had strengthened the state’s commitment to preparedness. She cited investments in a Biosafety Level 3 laboratory and biobank at the Infectious Disease Hospital, Yaba, alongside intensified surveillance and healthcare workers’ training. In his keynote address, Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic), Lagos State University of Science and Technology, Prof. Abiodun Denloye, identified poor sanitation, unsafe water, inadequate housing and environmental degradation as factors worsening disease vulnerability in African cities. He advocated stronger environmental protection, disease surveillance, resilient urban planning, community protection and One Health governance. Also, GET Consortium’s Chief Operating Officer, Dr. Ayodotun Bobadoye, called for sustained investment in laboratory infrastructure, border monitoring, workforce development and community engagement. Director General, Nigerian Institute of Medical Research (NIMR), Prof. John Obafunwa, urged increased local investment in medical research, genomic sequencing, vaccine development and domestic production of essential medical supplies to reduce Africa’s dependence on imports. The conference brought together policymakers, researchers and health professionals to strengthen Africa’s preparedness against emerging biological threats. news.content_title: Lagos Seeks Africa-Wide Bioshield Alliance As Experts Advocate Stronger Surveillance, Research
news.content: Home News Entertainment Politics Sports Business iSaturday iSunday Editorial Columnist Search Search Home News Entertainment Politics Sports Business iSaturday iSunday Editorial Columnist Saturday, November 28, 2026 Search Search Home News Entertainment Politics Sports Business iSaturday iSunday Editorial Columnist Copyright 2021 - All Right Reserved Home NewsHealthLagos Seeks Africa-Wide Bioshield Alliance As Experts Advocate Stronger Surveillance, Research HealthLatest News Lagos Seeks Africa-Wide Bioshield Alliance As Experts Advocate Stronger Surveillance, Research by Chioma Umeha November 25, 2026 written by Chioma Umeha November 25, 2026 Share 0FacebookTwitterPinterestEmail 0 •••Unveils Digital Bioshield To Combat Emerging Disease Threats Lagos State Government has unveiled an innovative digital biosecurity framework, known as the Lagos State Bioshield, designed to detect, monitor and contain emerging infectious disease threats without disrupting economic activities and the movement of people in the state. The initiative, which integrates artificial intelligence (AI), telemedicine and digital health surveillance, is aimed at keeping Lagos open for business while strengthening its capacity to withstand biological emergencies. The initiative was unveiled by the Commissioner for Health, Prof. Akin Abayomi, at the 11th African Conference on One Health and Biosecurity, organised by the Lagos State Ministry of Health in partnership with the Global Emerging Pathogens Treatment Consortium (GET Consortium), on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos. The conference was themed, “Bio-Shielding Africa’s Megacities Against Emerging Threats: The Lagos State Story.” Speaking on the theme, Prof. Abayomi explained that the Bioshield framework was developed from lessons learnt during the Ebola outbreak and COVID-19 pandemic, particularly the need to balance public health protection with economic sustainability. He noted that shutting down Lagos during a public health emergency could have devastating consequences, considering that approximately 70 per cent of residents depend on daily earnings for their livelihoods. According to him, the Bioshield is designed to ensure that businesses, tourism, social activities and everyday livelihoods continue even during public health emergencies. He identified Lassa fever, dengue, yellow fever, Marburg virus disease and Ebola, alongside genetically modified and emerging unknown pathogens, as biological threats requiring specialised preparedness and response capabilities. The Commissioner identified Lagos’ high population density, rapid urbanisation, extensive domestic and international travel, migration, sanitation challenges and large informal settlements as factors that increase its vulnerability to infectious disease outbreaks. He disclosed that Lagos has an estimated population of about 30.1 million, with an average population density of approximately 6,800 persons per square kilometre, while some local government areas exceed 20,000 persons per square kilometre. He further highlighted the risks associated with the movement of people, livestock and agricultural products into the state, noting that Lagos receives approximately 70 per cent of Nigeria’s international air traffic. He disclosed that the state receives about 1.8 million cattle annually, underscoring the need to extend biosecurity measures beyond human health to include animal and environmental health under the One Health approach. Explaining the operational framework, Prof. Abayomi said the Lagos State Bioshield has two major components: an outer layer that identifies potential biological threats associated with people entering the state and an inner layer that monitors individuals who may develop symptoms after arrival. Its Health Radar platform enables the registration and monitoring of travellers and participants at major events, using WhatsApp, SMS and email to conduct daily health checks for up to 21 days. He added that individuals reporting symptoms are connected to telemedicine services for initial medical assessment, with referrals, laboratory investigations and specialised interventions activated where necessary. The system also uses artificial intelligence to support risk classification and escalation of suspected high-risk cases to the Ministry of Health and relevant public health authorities, with the objective of identifying concerning cases within 24 hours of symptom reporting, where possible. Highlighting the successful pilot deployment during the recently concluded CANEX WKND, the Commissioner disclosed that the Bioshield system monitored approximately 19,000 registered delegates, including 2,298 international visitors, amid concerns about the Ebola outbreak in Central Africa and the possibility of imported infections. The exercise recorded 2,454 telemedicine consultations, 241 clinical referrals and 219 individuals flagged for further attention, while 22.6 per cent of respondents reported symptoms requiring assessment. All identified cases were followed up and closed out, with no severe outcome associated with the suspected high-consequence infections reported. Prof. Abayomi disclosed that the state was working towards Bioshield 3.0, which would strengthen the technology’s artificial intelligence and telemedicine capabilities, improve integration with airports and major event venues, establish sustainable financing arrangements and provide a stronger legal framework. He added that plans were underway to integrate the platform with the Lagos State Smart Health Information Platform (SHIP), while exploring travel insurance and event-based financing options to support its long-term sustainability. In her remarks, the Special Adviser to the Governor on Health, Dr. (Mrs.) Kemi Ogunyemi, described Lagos as a critical gateway for biological threats entering Africa, given its population, international airport, seaports and major commercial markets. She stressed that protecting Lagos was essential to strengthening Africa’s health security, noting that human, animal and environmental health were interconnected and required coordinated action. Dr. Ogunyemi disclosed that Lagos had strengthened its disease surveillance systems, Emergency Operations Centre and collaboration among human health practitioners, veterinary doctors and environmental officers. She also highlighted the Lagos One Health Strategy, approved by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, which provides a coordinated platform for the health, agriculture and environment sectors. She called for the establishment of a continental BioShield Alliance involving megacities such as Lagos, Cairo, Kinshasa, Johannesburg and Nairobi to promote data sharing, joint training and common preparedness standards. Earlier, the Permanent Secretary, Lagos State Ministry of Health, Dr. (Mrs.) Dayo Lajide, said the state’s experience during the 2014 Ebola outbreak and COVID-19 pandemic had reinforced the need for sustained investment in preparedness. She noted that Lagos had strengthened its biosecurity infrastructure, including its Biosafety Level 3 laboratory and biobank at the Infectious Disease Hospital, Yaba, while activating emergency preparedness structures, intensifying surveillance and training healthcare workers following the declaration of the Ebola outbreak in Central Africa. She described the successful hosting of CANEX WKND, with over 19,247 registered delegates, as evidence of the state’s growing preparedness capacity. In his keynote address, Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) of Lagos State University of Science and Technology, Prof. Abiodun Denloye, identified inadequate housing, poor ventilation, unsafe water, poor sanitation, blocked drainage channels, improper waste disposal and environmental degradation as major factors increasing disease vulnerability in rapidly growing African cities. He advocated a five-pillar urban bio-shielding framework encompassing environmental protection, disease intelligence and surveillance, resilient urban design, community protection and One Health governance. He also called for neighbourhood vulnerability mapping, improved primary healthcare, stronger laboratory capacity, vaccination, safe food and water systems, and training of health journalists to promote accurate public health reporting and counter misinformation. Also speaking, the Chief Operating Officer of GET Consortium, Dr. Ayodotun Bobadoye, said the conference was convened to assess Lagos State’s biosecurity capacity, identify existing gaps and develop a strategic framework for strengthening preparedness against emerging biological threats. He emphasised the importance of sustained investments in disease surveillance, laboratory infrastructure, border monitoring, environmental management, community engagement and workforce development, noting that biosecurity encompasses the protection of human, animal, plant and environmental health. He expressed the expectation that the deliberations would produce a Lagos biosecurity partnership strategy with short- and medium-term priorities. Presenting on strengthening medical research and innovation for emerging disease preparedness and response in Africa, the Director-General and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian Institute of Medical Research (NIMR), Prof. John Oladapo Obafunwa, called for increased investment in local medical research, genomic sequencing, vaccine development and domestic production of essential medical supplies. He identified inadequate research funding, weak institutional collaboration, shortages of skilled professionals and dependence on imported vaccines and diagnostics as major challenges to Africa’s preparedness. He urged stronger partnerships among government agencies, universities, research institutions and the private sector to translate scientific discoveries into practical healthcare solutions. The conference brought together policymakers, researchers, healthcare professionals, development partners, security agencies and other stakeholders to deliberate on strengthening Africa’s capacity to anticipate, prevent and respond to emerging biological threats. Speakers emphasised that effective biosecurity requires sustained government commitment, scientific innovation, community participation, inter-agency collaboration and regional cooperation to build resilient cities and safeguard public health.
